paras: The lynching of Sam Cornwall was the shooting death of a Black prisoner on a public road in Chester County, South Carolina, in the early morning of September 29 or 30, 1888, while he was in a constable's custody on a peace warrant. His guard said they were fired on from ambush and fled, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of parties unknown. Papers from New York to Texas carried the story, several of them blaming the officers who had left him.

According to a wire dispatch from Columbia, Cornwall had quarreled with a white man named Tom Smith, and a peace warrant was then sworn out against him and given to Constable Lipford to serve. The officer, called T. W. Lippford in the Chester report and a deputy sheriff named Lypford in The Sun, arrested Cornwall and set out at night to take him before a trial justice. The Sun put the trial justice's office about fifteen miles away, while the wire said the party started for the court house.

The guard numbered two men in The Sun's account and three in the Chester report and the wire, which said Tom Smith was among them. At about 4 o'clock in the morning, by the constable's account, the party was fired into from ambush and the officer and his guard fled, leaving Cornwall behind. Residents some distance from the road heard twelve or fifteen pistol shots and then three or four horses moving off rapidly, and The Sun added that more shots followed five minutes after the first.

After daylight a man driving to town found the body lying across the road with the hands tied together, about eight miles from Chester. The Sun said the deputy and his posse returned to the spot and found him there "riddled with bullets." Dr. Davega counted fifteen bullet holes, the same number the wire reported.

A coroner's inquest found that Cornwall died of gunshot wounds "inflicted by parties unknown to the constable and others." No arrests had been made when the Chester report was written, and Coroner Murphy was to push further investigation; the report added that a .45-calibre Winchester rifle had been used. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the later coverage.

The New York Sun printed the ambush version under the headline "Cowardly Officers Leave a Prisoner to the Mercy of Lynchers" and in its text called Lypford "the cowardly deputy." The Columbia wire, which said Cornwall was "brutally lynched," ran in the San Antonio Daily Light as "Negro Cruelly Lynched" and in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette under a headline stressing that "A Negro Quarrels With a White Man and is Killed While Under Arrest." The Indianapolis Journal headed the same wire "Negro Murdered by Peace Officers," treating the arresting party as the killers, though the text itself named no one.

In South Carolina, the Newberry Herald and News reprinted a Chester special as "Cowardly, Brutal Murder," the only account with the inquest verdict. The coverage ran from October 1 to October 4, 1888, and no Black-press account is available for this period.

The Chester special, dated September 29, placed the killing on the morning of that day, while The Sun's dispatch of September 30 and the wire of October 1 placed it a day later. The ambush story rests on what the constable and his guard reported, and the wire, which does not mention an ambush, left the arresting party, including Cornwall's antagonist Tom Smith, as the last men known to be with him.

reader.title: Lynching of Sam Cornwall
bases: A Black prisoner under arrest on a peace warrant was shot to death on a public road at night by armed men, and the papers called it a lynching (A1, A4, A5, A6).

Cornwall was killed without legal process while a bound prisoner (A1, A6), and the wire called it a lynching (A4, A5); the local report gives twelve to fifteen shots and three or four horses but no count of attackers, and no paper states the killers' motive beyond the wire's mention of his quarrel with a white man (A5, A6).

A Chester special (A6), a separate dispatch in The Sun (A1) and the Columbia wire (A2, A4, A5) agree that Cornwall was shot to death while under arrest on a peace warrant in Chester County, though they differ on the date, the guard and the circumstances.

accounts.label: Chester special
accounts.gist: Constable Lippford and a guard of three were fired into from ambush at 4 a.m. and fled; Cornwall was killed instantly, and the coroner's jury found he died at the hands of parties unknown.

accounts.label: The Sun's dispatch
accounts.gist: Deputy Lypford and a posse of two were fired on from ambush; they fled, more shots followed five minutes later, and they returned after daylight to find Cornwall dead with his hands tied.

accounts.label: Columbia wire
accounts.gist: After a quarrel with Tom Smith, Cornwall was arrested by Constable Lipford and three white men including Smith, who started for the court house; his body with fifteen bullets was found by the roadside next morning. No ambush is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'Cowardly Officers Leave a Prisoner to the Mercy of Lynchers' and called Lypford 'the cowardly deputy'.
The Indianapolis Journal headed the wire 'Negro Murdered by Peace Officers' and kept its 'brutally lynched'.
Texas papers ran the wire under 'Negro Cruelly Lynched' and 'South Carolina Lynching. A Negro Quarrels With a White Man and is Killed While Under Arrest'.
The Newberry Herald and News ran the Chester special as 'Cowardly, Brutal Murder'.

record_check.dossier: Contested: about 4 a.m. Sept. 29 by the local Chester special; Sept. 30 by The Sun and the wire.
Public road about eight miles from Chester.
Killing; no seizure is reported. He was shot from ambush (by the officer's account) after his guard fled, or killed after the constable's party left with him (wire).
Killed while a bound prisoner in the constable's custody; the guard fled rather than surrendering him.
Coroner's jury: parties unknown; the wire places his antagonist Tom Smith in the arresting party, and one headline blamed the 'Peace Officers'.
